We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-679)
response:
Activation steering works by injecting a direction vector into a model's residual stream at a chosen layer to induce or suppress a concept — but the central question here is whether a vector extracted at one layer retains its semantic effect when applied at another, and whether that degradation (or transformation) follows a predictable pattern tied to where the target concept sits in an abstraction hierarchy. The key concepts are: residual stream geometry (how representations accumulate and rotate across depth), concept abstraction level (sensory/syntactic features at early layers vs. relational/world-model features at late layers), vector drift (the angular and magnitude changes a steering vector undergoes as it propagates forward through attention and MLP sublayers), and the abstraction hierarchy hypothesis (the empirical regularity that low-level features like tone or syntax stabilize early, while high-level features like "royalty" or "deception" don't have stable linear representations until mid-to-late layers). The practical craft question is: if you extract a "deception" vector from layer 18 and inject it at layer 6, does it steer toward deception, toward some precursor representation of deception, or toward noise — and does that answer change systematically depending on the concept's abstractness? What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the superposition problem: early-layer residual stream directions are heavily entangled because the model is compressing many features into shared dimensions, so an injected vector targeting one high-level concept will likely activate unintended features, and the beginner interprets the messy behavioral output as "steering partially worked" when it actually reflects destructive interference with unrelated feature directions co-located in that subspace. The stakes are that without understanding drift patterns, steering-based interpretability and control methods have no principled basis for layer selection — you're tuning a dial you don't understand.

The prediction is that "banana" vectors extracted at mid-network layers will show high cosine similarity (likely above 0.85) to their own forward-propagated versions across subsequent layers, while "justice" vectors will show substantially lower and more variable similarity — potentially dropping below 0.5 within 4-6 layers — because concrete concepts have stable, largely feed-forward visual/lexical grounding that doesn't require progressive compositional elaboration. The mechanistic reason is that concrete concept representations are largely fixed after early MLP layers resolve token identity (Geva et al. 2022 showed MLP sublayers act as key-value memories that "write" factual associations into the residual stream early), whereas abstract concepts like "justice" are relational — their representation depends on contextual integration happening in attention heads at multiple depths, so the direction genuinely changes as more context is incorporated rather than merely scaling. A second asymmetry: "banana" drift, when it occurs, will be mostly magnitude change with preserved direction (the vector gets refined but not rotated), while "justice" drift will show true angular rotation because late attention heads are actively constructing the concept rather than retrieving it. Empirical support for this asymmetry comes indirectly from Hernandez et al. (2023) on relational vs. entity representations in ROME/MEMIT, and from the logit lens work (nostalgebraist 2020) where concrete token predictions crystallize in early layers while abstract attribute predictions remain fluid until the final third of the network. The dangerous implication for steering is that injecting a "justice" vector extracted at layer 20 into layer 8 of GPT2-XL or Llama-2-13B isn't just early — you're injecting a compositionally complete representation into a layer that hasn't yet assembled the contextual prerequisites that make that direction meaningful, which is categorically different from what happens with "banana."

(2021) and related BERTology studies consistently find that high-frequency abstract terms with narrow collocational entropy show earlier layer "lock-in" on probing tasks than low-frequency abstract terms with broad contextual distributions, which is exactly what collapse of the drift asymmetry would predict. The unsettling implication is that your steering vector extraction experiment would produce a false negative — "justice" looks stable, you conclude abstract concepts are steerable from early layers, but what you've actually measured is the model's compressed stereotype of justice-as-legal-apparatus, not justice-as-normative-concept. A clean diagnostic is to compare drift profiles for "justice" in legal corpora contexts versus philosophical corpora contexts within the same model: if the vector direction diverges substantially between those two prompt distributions at the same layer, you're measuring corpus statistics; if it converges, you might have something more genuinely abstract. response:
The layer-transfer problem relocates rather than dissolves, and the specific failure mode you hit first is feature interaction collapse: when you activate an SAE feature for, say, "fairness-assertion" at layer 8 that was learned at layer 20, the downstream MLP sublayers at layers 9-12 have never been trained to receive that feature in an active state at that position in the computational sequence, so they treat it as an anomalous input and either suppress it via effective learned gating or compose it with co-occurring features in ways the SAE dictionary never encoded. Bricken et al. (2023) demonstrated that even in one-layer models, SAE features interact non-additively — activating two features simultaneously produces residual stream directions not predictable from the sum of individual feature vectors — and this interaction problem compounds with depth because each MLP layer is implicitly a learned function of which features are co-active, not just which features are present. The situation is worse for abstract concepts specifically because their SAE features at late layers tend to be high-order conjunctions — the "justice" feature at layer 22 might only be meaningful when co-active with a "negation" feature and an "institutional" feature, and transplanting it to layer 8 without its required co-features means you're activating an incomplete conjunction that has no interpretable behavioral correlate. What you'd observe experimentally is not clean failure but corrupted partial effects: the model's output would show weak, inconsistent nudges toward justice-adjacent content mixed with non-sequitur activations of whatever early-layer features happen to be geometrically proximal to the transplanted direction in that layer's dictionary. The deeper diagnosis this forces is that SAE decomposition solves the superposition readability problem but doesn't solve the computational dependency problem — features are nodes in a DAG, and transplanting a node without its upstream dependencies is still incoherent, just now incoherent in a more legible way.

Yes, a minimum coherent bundle almost certainly exists, and the right framework for thinking about it is not a flat set but a partial order — some features are load-bearing prerequisites that gate the meaningful activation of others, while some are co-expressive elaborations that can be dropped without destroying coherence, and distinguishing these two classes is the actual hard problem. The most tractable empirical approach without exhaustive search is causal scrubbing (Chan et al. 2022), adapted for SAE feature space: you systematically replace subsets of co-active features with their "clean" baseline activations and measure behavioral degradation, using the degradation curve's shape to identify prerequisite features (removal causes sharp cliff) versus elaborative features (removal causes gradual slope). A second approach exploits the correlation structure of SAE feature activations across a large prompt distribution — features that are nearly always co-active with your target feature across diverse contexts are bundle candidates, while features that co-activate only in specific corpus registers are likely stereotyping artifacts rather than genuine prerequisites, giving you a corpus-statistics filter before you run any interventions. The practical number here matters: Templeton et al. (2024) in Anthropic's scaling SAE work found that many interpretable features in Claude have co-activation clusters of 3-8 strongly correlated features, suggesting minimum bundles for mid-abstraction concepts are likely in that range — small enough to be tractable but large enough that naive single-feature steering will routinely fail. The failure mode that tells you you've found the bundle boundary is a phase transition in behavioral coherence rather than linear improvement: adding the nth prerequisite feature produces a qualitative jump in output coherence disproportionate to its individual activation weight, because you've crossed the threshold where the receiving layers' implicit gating conditions are jointly satisfied.

The evidence suggests the prerequisite structure is non-arbitrary and systematically skewed toward specific head types, but the mapping is probabilistic rather than clean: load-bearing prerequisite features disproportionately originate from heads performing binding and entity-tracking operations — what Olsson et al. (2022) called induction heads generalize into a broader class of "structure-building" heads that copy and compose relational information across token positions, and these heads' outputs appear repeatedly as prerequisites because they establish the referential scaffolding that abstract concept features are built on top of. Concretely, in the IOI (indirect object identification) circuit work (Wang et al. 2022), the S-inhibition heads and name-mover heads form a strict functional dependency — you cannot get coherent name-moving behavior without prior S-inhibition, which is exactly the prerequisite partial order structure applied to a specific circuit — suggesting this isn't coincidental but reflects how transformers factorize relational computation across depth. The mechanistic reason prerequisite features cluster at binding/induction heads rather than, say, previous-token heads is that previous-token heads write local positional information that MLPs can use opportunistically but don't strictly depend on, whereas binding heads write cross-positional relational structure that downstream MLP computations for abstract concepts literally cannot reconstruct from the residual stream alone if it's absent. Where the picture gets messier is that some prerequisite features trace back to MLP sublayers rather than attention heads — Geva et al. (2023) showed that MLP layers perform "attribute extraction" that feeds subsequent attention-based composition, creating mixed prerequisite chains that cross head/MLP boundaries and resist clean architectural assignment. The practical upshot for bundle transplantation is partially encouraging: if load-bearing prerequisites cluster at identifiable head types, you can use head attribution methods (activation patching per head, as in path patching from Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2023) to efficiently identify which heads' outputs must be included in the bundle, reducing the search space from all SAE features to the output subspace of a small number of functionally characterized head classes.

The positional context dependency is likely the harder constraint, and here's the precise reason: feature co-activation dependencies are satisfied by what you inject, but positional context dependencies are satisfied by what the model has already written into the residual stream at specific sequence positions before your intervention layer, and you cannot retroactively populate those positions without re-running the earlier layers on different inputs — the intervention is downstream of the information it needs. Concretely, when a binding head at layer 15 computes a query-key match between a subject token at position 3 and an object token at position 11, that match writes a relational feature into the residual stream at position 11 that encodes "this token is bound to position 3's referent" — if you transplant a feature bundle to layer 8 that assumes this binding has occurred, the layer 8 residual stream at position 11 simply doesn't contain that positional relationship yet, and no amount of feature injection at a single position recovers it because the binding is a joint property of two positions simultaneously. The empirical signature of this failure mode is position-selective behavioral corruption: your intervention would produce coherent effects on prompts where the relevant entities are local or repeated (binding heads have short attention distances to work with) but degrade specifically on prompts requiring long-distance binding, which is a clean experimental dissociation from feature co-activation failures that would be position-agnostic. Hanna et al. (2023) on the greater-than circuit and Davies et al. on positional encodings both show that certain computations are gated on positional relationships being resolvable within the attention pattern, not just on features being present — the circuit simply doesn't fire correctly if the key positional relationships fall outside its effective attention window or haven't been established yet. This suggests a hierarchy of constraint hardness: feature co-activation dependencies can in principle be satisfied by bundle injection, positional context dependencies require either early-layer intervention (before binding heads run) or full sequence-level intervention, and this makes abstract concept steering fundamentally harder for long-document or multi-entity contexts than for short, locally-grounded prompts.

response:
The directionality asymmetry is real but the conclusion isn't quite "downward transfers are viable, upward aren't" — it's more precise to say that downward transfers inject underspecified representations into layers that will attempt to complete them, while upward transfers inject overspecified representations into layers that lack the prerequisites to interpret them, and underspecification is recoverable while overspecification generally isn't. This maps directly onto an induction/suppression asymmetry: suppression interventions work by canceling a direction in the residual stream, which is a purely local algebraic operation that doesn't depend on positional context or feature prerequisites being satisfied — you're subtracting a vector, not activating a computational pathway — which is why Turner et al. (2023) found activation addition for suppression goals (reducing "banana" completions) was more robust across injection layers than induction goals requiring the model to generate content from an injected concept. Induction is harder precisely because it requires the injected representation to propagate forward and successfully recruit downstream computational machinery — attention heads must pattern-match against it, MLPs must compose with it — and that recruitment process is what fails when positional context is absent or prerequisites aren't met, whereas suppression just needs the direction to persist in the residual stream long enough to reduce logit probability on target tokens, which is a much weaker requirement. There's a further asymmetry within induction itself: injecting a concrete concept early (downward transfer of a "banana" representation to layer 2) likely succeeds because the receiving layers will elaborate it using normal processing, while injecting an abstract concept early fails because the elaboration requires positional context that won't exist yet — so downward transfer is viable for induction only when the concept's computational dependencies are satisfiable by the layers below the injection point. The practical implication, which interpretability work hasn't cleanly confronted, is that robust concept induction via steering may require distributed intervention — injecting partial representations at multiple layers timed to when each prerequisite computation completes — rather than single-point injection, which would explain why empirical steering results show such high variance across prompt types that differ in entity structure and binding complexity.
